newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Riaupulp asset sale affects equity, bond holders.
newsitem.headline: Riaupulp asset sale affects equity, bond holders.

text.p: Riau Andalan Pulp must consider the effect its planned asset sales would have on its shareholders as well as its bondholders, company finance director W. Michael Verge told Reuters Financial Television.

Riaupulp, which is 98.9 percent held by Asia Pacific Resources International, recently created a furor among bond investors by announcing asset sales that would trigger a mandatory redemption of US$300 million worth of outstanding RAPP International Finance notes.

"Obviously, we have concerns with investor relations but we also want investors to understand that part of those investors are equity holders that might have a deep say in actions that could possibly harm them," Verge told RFTV in an interview.
"And to date, anyway, no organization that represents a majority of the bondholders has approached us," he said.

Indenture forms on US$300 million of outstanding Yankee bonds of Rapp International Finance oblige Riaupulp to retire all of its oustanding secured debt at 101 percent of the principal amount if collateral sales exceed 25 percent of the book value of the collateral.
Riaupulp has sold a power plant and plans to sell a chemical manufacturing facility that are part of its paper pulp mill complex in Riau province, Sumatra, Indonesia.
Sale of the chemical facility would trigger the bond redemption.
PT Inti Indorayon Utama, another April group member, has offered to buy Riaupulp's chemical assets, subject to shareholder approval.
Verge said he expects the sale to go forward, probably by the end of February.

Prior to the asset sale announcement, US$100 million of 11.5 percent RAPP International bonds due in 2000 were trading at 105 percent of par and another US$200 million of 13.25 percent bonds due in 2005 were trading at 111.
By calling the bonds at 101, bondholders gains would be slashed by some US$24 million, traders said.
Since the announcement, bids for the bond have fallen to 101, while offers have disappeared, they said.
Asked if Riaupulp might amend the bond redemption clause before the expected asset sale in February, Verge said "in my personal opinion, that (decision) can't come from us".

He said that as a registered company under U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) rules and as a unit of a U.S.-listed company, Riaupulp must abide by "full and fair disclosure" regulations and honor the letter of its contracts.
He also noted that not calling the bonds would leave the company, and bondholders, in more difficult straits.
"We would probably be in more difficult circumstances because we would probably default on the bond, breach the indenture and in that case redemption would be at 100," he said.
Bondholders have charged that the asset sales are unneccessary. But Verge said the sales would increase the company's return on assets.
"We would have a much stronger balance sheet," he said.
Verge said the bond redemption clause had been included in the bond contract to protect investors and was clearly spelled out in the prospectus and indenture.
"I sometimes wonder if the bonds were trading at 95 or 96 whether bond traders wouldn't be pushing us to redeem at 101 rather than asking us not to," he said.
